title: The Secret Skills of Master Teachers
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This is Stuart's response to reading James Clear's Atomic Habits, which he treats less as a habits book than as an account of how careers and lives end up where nobody planned. He distils six lessons: behaviour is driven by both environmental cues and internal emotion, the habits that matter most are easy to ignore, small daily gains compound, tiny errors at home accumulate into toxic results, systems beat goals, and beneath behaviour lie beliefs. He illustrates each with his own practice, from compulsive email checking to a refusal to build a career at the cost of his wife and children. The piece closes by tying the last lesson to his own work on student beliefs, which he argues is where a teacher should start in changing achievement outcomes. It is part of his series on how teachers make decisions today that yield mastery later.
points: Stuart uses his own habit of checking email 10 to 20 times a day to show how environment and emotional state jointly drive behaviour, making Clear's framework concrete for a teacher.
He argues that daily twenty-minute complaining sessions in the copy room do not cost much today but, compounded over a decade, reshape both one's productivity and one's character.
The 1% arithmetic (about 38% better in a year versus nearly zero if 1% worse daily) supports the claim that small invisible habits determine outcomes.
His takeaway on systems over goals is applied to his own AP and general-level courses, where the pass-rate target matters less than the homework, feedback and test-design systems behind it.
He links Clear's claim that beliefs sit at the core of behaviour to his own thesis that raising student achievement starts with cultivating student beliefs.
quotes: Here's the thing: I'm not huge into the literature on habits these days. I've been fascinated by it before, but I've kind of moved on. So when I sat down to read Atomic Habits, it wasn't because I was intrigued by the topic — it was because of how much I've appreciated Clear's clarity of thought, earnestness, and writer's ability over the past few years.

As it turned out, Atomic Habits wasn't just a book on habits for me. Rather, it was an exploration of how our lives and careers end up in places that we didn't expect. What does it really take to achieve our biggest goals — for example, the construction of flourishing and impactful lives, professionally and personally? Clear gave me needed insight into this large, hairy, burning question.

Why did I used to do that, even when I knew email is so infrequently connected to the long-term flourishing outcomes of my students — or of me? It's a mixture. My environment made it easy because I had email on my phone, and my often sub-optimal internal state made it appealing. Whenever I'm stressed or overwhelmed or feeling pressured, the draw of my inbox is stronger.
But doing that every day for the next ten years costs me hugely. It changes the shape of my life.

For the past six months or so, I've been aggressively trying to bend my life to work within sharper constraints than I've ever placed on it. Why? Because I don't want to build a successful teaching or writing career at the cost of consistently neglecting my wife and children. It's an unacceptable cost.

Plenty of us set goals. Clear essentially says this is pointless. If you set a goal to win a championship, that's fine, but it's how you approach practice and coaching and recruiting and so on — those systems are where you're going to win or lose championships.

At the core of behavior, you'll find beliefs. I love this because it lines up with the central argument of Chapter 2 in These 6 Things and the entirety of the Student Motivation Course. If we want our kids to do work and do it with care — we do — then we need to get so much better at cultivating five key beliefs in all of our kids. This is manageable at the school or classroom level, but almost no one is doing it.
